summary: The developer machine has the Python runtime, node/npx, Docker, az (signed-in), and the DocumentDB MCP server plus a rich set of documentdb-* skills required to build the Python LangChain multi-agent sample against the live cluster. Infra tooling for IaC (bicep, terraform) and developer shells (mongosh) are missing but not blocking. Several cold answers in the prompt review described Cosmos DB patterns (RUs, databaseAccounts, port 10255) or general MongoDB syntax; installed skills (documentdb-azure-deployment, documentdb-vector-search, documentdb-local-deployment, documentdb-security, documentdb-full-text-search, documentdb-driver) provide definitive, service-specific guidance to correct these confusions. Remaining gaps are the sample's AI model choices and a few exact schema decisions the skills do not prescribe; the build can start with reasonable defaults but the builder must choose and document these.
summary_points: All runtime and MCP tooling required to build and verify the sample are present (python, pip, node/npx, docker, az signed-in, the 'documentdb' MCP server and the DocumentDB agent skills).

Key cold-answer confusions were detected: resource type and CLI for clusters (Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters), capacity model (compute tiers like M10/M30 vs RUs), connection-string shape (global.mongocluster host + TLS + retryWrites=false), vector index API (`cosmosSearch` / vector-diskann / HNSW / IVF), full-text search via createSearchIndexes + $search, local gateway image (port 10260), and Entra ID (OIDC/MONGODB-OIDC) support — all corrected with skill docs or Learn results.
The build is ready to begin, but some accelerators and CLI tools that speed IaC or manual checks are absent (bicep, terraform, mongosh); these are recommended but not required.

Critical information not present in any installed skill or docs: which embedding model and LLM to use for the LangChain agents, exact document schemas and sample-data size—these are builder decisions that must be recorded in README/.env.example.
No MCP server or skill needed for data-plane verification is missing — the 'documentdb' MCP server is available and will let the builder inspect collections, indexes and explain plans.

confusions.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Top-level resource type (account): Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (API-specific child resources: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts/mongodbDatabases and /mongoCollections in some ARM versions).
confusions.grounded_answer: The correct top-level deployment resource type for Azure DocumentDB clusters is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (API versions listed in the skill); DocumentDB clusters are deployed as mongoClusters, not as Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Historic overlap with Cosmos DB and older Azure samples: many Cosmos DB quickstarts use Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts, so a model trained on older Cosmos samples will suggest databaseAccounts instead of the new mongoClusters resource for this service.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder used databaseAccounts / Cosmos quickstarts they would attempt to provision or manage the wrong resource type (Cosmos DB account) and fail to create or configure the managed DocumentDB mongoClusters or create incompatible resources.
improvements: Add a prominent note on any Learn landing page and the documentdb-azure-deployment README: 'Use Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (not databaseAccounts) to deploy Azure DocumentDB clusters.'
Update any agent skill snippets that still show databaseAccounts to call out mongoClusters for the managed DocumentDB product.

confusions.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the built-in az cosmosdb command group (core CLI). Example to create a Mongo-compatible account: az cosmosdb create --name myDocDbAccount --resource-group myRg --locations regionName=eastus --kind MongoDB
confusions.grounded_answer: The current deployment and recommended path for DocumentDB clusters is to deploy the Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters resource (Bicep/ARM/Terraform) or to use az resource create / az deployment group create with the mongoClusters resource-type and API version. There is no simple az cosmosdb subgroup command that provisions mongoClusters as a first-class one-liner; the skill recommends Bicep or az resource create against Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters.

grounding_links.title: Example: deploy mongoClusters with az resource create (skill example)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The az cosmosdb command group is the standard for Azure Cosmos DB account management; a model exposed mainly to Cosmos content will assume the same az group applies to this managed Mongo offering.

confusion_sources.title: az cosmosdb quickstarts (Cosmos DB account docs)

confusions.build_risk: Using az cosmosdb create would attempt to create or manage a Cosmos DB account and not the mongoClusters resource; deployment steps, defaults and available options would be incorrect for the target product.
improvements: Document in the top-level quickstart that the DocumentDB cluster is deployed as Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters and provide the exact az resource create sample (or Bicep) instead of suggesting az cosmosdb.
Add an inline note in `az cosmosdb` docs pointing to `Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters` for customers seeking the new managed Mongo cluster product.

confusions.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Bicep/ARM resource type: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (e.g. resource cosmos 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts@2021-04-15' = { name: 'myAccount' ... } ). Terraform resource: azurerm_cosmosdb_account (provider azurerm) with kind = "MongoDB" and appropriate capabilities/settings.
confusions.grounded_answer: Bicep/ARM should target Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (API versions such as 2025-09-01 etc.); Terraform via the AzureRM provider uses azurerm_mongo_cluster (or the azapi/azurerm resource that maps to Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters). Do not use databaseAccounts/azurerm_cosmosdb_account for the managed DocumentDB mongoClusters resource.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Terraform and Bicep examples for Cosmos DB accounts are common in earlier docs—models trained on those examples will suggest azurerm_cosmosdb_account and databaseAccounts even though the new mongoClusters resource is the correct target.
confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong resource type (databaseAccounts / azurerm_cosmosdb_account) will provision the wrong Azure resource and will not give the expected DocumentDB cluster features (mongoClusters properties), causing deployment failure or mismatched runtime behaviour.
improvements: Add a short example Bicep snippet using Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters to the top-level Quickstart so builders copying examples don't pick databaseAccounts.
Make Azure CLI / Terraform provider docs link to the dedicated mongoClusters resource as the authoritative method to deploy this managed Mongo service.

confusions.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
confusions.cold_answer: Use a Mongo URI (SRV or standard). SRV form: mongodb+srv://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com/<dbname>?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false. Non-SRV form: mongodb://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/<dbname>?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false. Port (non-SRV) is 10255 and SSL must be enabled (ssl=true). retryWrites is typically false for Cosmos Mongo compatibility.
confusions.grounded_answer: For Azure DocumentDB clusters the connection string typically uses the mongodb+srv scheme and a host under the cluster's global host (skill shows example: mongodb+srv://<user>:<password>@<cluster>.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com/?tls=true&authMechanism=SCRAM-SHA-256&retrywrites=false). TLS/`tls=true` (or tls param) must be enabled and retryWrites=false is recommended. The hostname suffix and some query keys differ from Cosmos DB for MongoDB accounts; rely on the cluster's Connection strings pane or the documentdb-azure-deployment guidance.

grounding_links.title: Example connection string and notes (skill reference)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The host suffix, port and query options given match Azure Cosmos DB's older Mongo API examples (`*.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255`) and not the new DocumentDB cluster hostnames and conventions (`*.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com` and tls query keys). The two services are Mongo-compatible but expose different connection endpoints and query parameters.

confusion_sources.title: Cosmos DB for MongoDB connection string docs (example showing :10255 and mongo.cosmos.azure.com)

confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong host suffix or port will cause authentication/connectivity errors or attempts to connect to a different Azure service (Cosmos DB). Mis-specified authMechanism/tls parameters can lead to driver errors (e.g., retryable-writes-related failures).
improvements: In the get-started quickstart emphasize the exact connection-string host suffix format and show both SRV and non-SRV correct examples for mongoClusters.
Add an agent-skill snippet that prints the cluster's connection-string template (with placeholders) to avoid copying Cosmos DB examples.

confusions.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
confusions.cold_answer: Capacity is managed at the Cosmos DB account level. Typical Cosmos models are provisioned throughput measured in Request Units/sec (RUs) and autoscale RUs; there is also a serverless option for some accounts. Some managed Mongo offerings expose instance/compute tiers (M-series/vCores) in addition to RU-based billing, but the mainstream Azure model is provisioned RUs (or serverless).
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB clusters are sized by compute tier (M-series: M10, M20, M30, ...), storage per-shard, and HA options — the skill explicitly lists compute tiers as the primary capacity knobs (M10–M200). This is a compute-tier (vCore-like) model for this product rather than Cosmos DB's RU model.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Many Azure database products (Cosmos DB core API) are billed in RUs; the model conflated Cosmos DB's RU model with the managed DocumentDB cluster which is billed/picked by compute tier (M-series).
confusions.build_risk: If a builder designs the sample assuming RUs they may pick incorrect index / query patterns or attempt to set throughput via RU settings that don't apply to mongoClusters; provisioning calls would fail or be ignored.
improvements: Add a short comparison table on the quickstart: 'Cosmos DB (RUs) vs Azure DocumentDB mongoClusters (compute tiers M-series)', and surface it in the agent skill outputs.

confusions.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
confusions.cold_answer: Primary authentication for the Mongo API is username/password (Mongo users created on the account; SCRAM). Cosmos/Mongo accounts also expose primary keys for SQL API; Azure AD (Microsoft Entra) authentication is available for some Cosmos APIs but is not the default for the Mongo wire protocol. If Azure AD were supported for Mongo, the driver would use an access token obtained from Entra ID and pass it as the password or via SASL/OAUTHBEARER mechanism, but in practice use username/password (SCRAM) for drivers.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) + RBAC for authentication; applications can use managed identities and OIDC-based auth (the skill shows examples with authMechanism like MONGODB-OIDC or a driver's documented OIDC mechanism). SCRAM (username/password / secondary users) remains supported for legacy or isolated scenarios, but Entra + RBAC is the preferred production pattern.

grounding_links.title: Use Microsoft Entra ID and role-based access control

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Older Cosmos Mongo API docs and some migration guides emphasize SCRAM/username passwords; the model conservatively described SCRAM as primary and was uncertain about Entra support. The DocumentDB service explicitly supports Entra ID/OIDC and prefers managed identities in many production scenarios.

confusion_sources.title: Older Cosmos MongoDB docs that emphasize SCRAM

confusions.build_risk: Assuming only SCRAM/passwords will lead the builder to store long-lived secrets instead of using managed identities and OIDC; this increases operational and security risk.
improvements: Add an 'Authentication quick reference' to documentdb-security that shows the driver configuration snippet for managed identities (MONGODB-OIDC) and the SCRAM secondary-user pattern for comparison.
Expose a short `documentdb-mcp-credentials` command that shows recommended connection-string templates for both SCRAM and Entra/OIDC modes.

confusions.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the official MongoDB drivers for your language (for Python, use pymongo). Do not use the Azure Cosmos SDK for Mongo-programmed workloads; the Mongo wire protocol is served so use mongodb-compatible client libraries.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct. Use standard MongoDB drivers (pymongo for Python). There is no separate service-specific application SDK that replaces the MongoDB drivers for the Mongo-compatible API; follow the driver best practices (singleton MongoClient, pooling) from the documentdb-driver skill.

confusions.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
confusions.cold_answer: Vector/index types exposed on Mongo-compatible Azure DocumentDB variants are not the same as native MongoDB indexes; recent managed clusters advertise HNSW, IVF and DiskANN. A plausible create-index call (Mongo shell-like) is: db.myCollection.createIndex({ embedding: 'vector' }, { algorithm: 'hnsw', dims: 1536, distance: 'cosine' }). Note: exact option names (algorithm, dims, distance) depend on the service extension; this is the form I'd attempt first.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB exposes vector indexes through the `cosmosSearch` index kind. Supported sub-types include vector-diskann, vector-hnsw and vector-ivf. Index creation uses `createIndex` with `cosmosSearchOptions` (e.g. kind: 'vector-diskann', dimensions: 1536, similarity: 'COS', plus tuning params like maxDegree and lBuild). The option keys differ from generic 'algorithm' / 'dims' names — use cosmosSearchOptions and the exact keys documented in the documentdb-vector-search skill.

grounding_links.title: Vector search — DiskANN index creation (skill reference)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer proposed a generic MongoDB 'vector' index syntax and option names that are common in some vector DBs or community extensions. Azure DocumentDB uses a provider-specific `cosmosSearch` index with `cosmosSearchOptions` and named kinds (vector-diskann, vector-hnsw, vector-ivf).

confusion_sources.title: Community examples using different vector-index syntaxes

confusions.build_risk: Attempting to create a vector index with the wrong option names or index kind will either fail or create a non-vector index; queries expecting vector search (cosmosSearch) would return wrong results or errors.
improvements: Add explicit createIndex examples in the agent skill documentation showing `cosmosSearchOptions` and sample parameters for the common embedding model (e.g., 1536 dims).
Surface the required field names in the MCP server index-creation helper so agents produce syntactically-correct createIndex commands.

confusions.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
confusions.cold_answer: Full-text/hybrid search is typically provided by integrating with Azure Cognitive Search (Azure Search) for Cosmos DB. For Mongo-like vector+text hybrid search you either use the provider's built-in vector index + text index if available, or combine a text index (Azure Search or service-specific search extension) with the vector index in the application to do hybrid ranking.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB provides built-in full-text search via createSearchIndexes and the $search aggregation stage (BM25 scoring). Hybrid BM25 + vector retrieval is supported through the built-in search features (the skill documents Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) and combining BM25 with cosmosSearch vector results). You do not need a separate Azure Cognitive Search service for the Mongo-compatible DocumentDB's native search + vector capabilities.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Older Cosmos or multi-service patterns often show integrating Cosmos DB with Azure Cognitive Search for rich text features; that pattern caused the answer to suggest an external search service rather than the built-in createSearchIndexes + $search approach documented for DocumentDB.

confusion_sources.title: Common Cosmos DB + Azure Cognitive Search integration docs

confusions.build_risk: If the builder wired an external Azure Cognitive Search pipeline they'd add unnecessary ETL, cost, and complexity, and they'd miss native $search+vector features that allow simpler, single-collection hybrid queries.
improvements: Add a short 'When to use external Azure Cognitive Search' section to the documentdb-full-text-search skill to prevent blanket recommendations to use Cognitive Search.
Provide a template RRF example combining $search BM25 results and cosmosSearch vector results in the skill resources.

confusions.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
confusions.cold_answer: Managed Azure Mongo-compatible accounts advertise a supported MongoDB server wire protocol version (commonly 4.2/5.0/6.0/7.0 depending on account). Expect most core CRUD and aggregation pipeline features to work, but some server-side features (server-side JS, all admin commands, certain change-stream/transaction semantics, or unsupported aggregation stages) may be missing or limited. Verify the exact supported server version on the account.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports multiple MongoDB wire-protocol/server versions (the migration docs and deployment skill indicate support for MongoDB server versions such as 5.0, 6.0, 7.0 and 8.0 depending on cluster configuration). The exact supported feature set is documented per cluster/server-version and some advanced or admin-only commands may differ; the skill and Learn pages list supported operators and compatibility guidance.

grounding_links.title: Which MongoDB versions does Azure DocumentDB support? (Learn doc excerpt)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The model hedged on supported versions and feature omissions because MongoDB server versions and feature parity differ by cluster/server version—this needs exact per-cluster verification. The service supports modern versions (5–8) but the exact set depends on the cluster's serverVersion setting.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes features present in a newer Mongo server but the target cluster runs an older supported serverVersion, certain aggregation stages or admin commands might fail at runtime.
improvements: Add a short skill command or MCP helper that reports the cluster's supported serverVersion and a compatibility summary so agents can verify the runtime target before generating queries that depend on newer features.

confusions.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
confusions.cold_answer: There is no full-featured local emulator for the Mongo-compatible Azure service. For local development run the official MongoDB Docker image (example: docker run -p 27017:27017 --name local-mongo -d mongo:7) and connect on port 27017. For testing against the real service use the cluster in DOCUMENTDB_URI.
confusions.grounded_answer: There is a supported local DocumentDB Gateway image (ghcr.io/documentdb/documentdb/documentdb-local:latest) intended for development; it exposes the MongoDB wire protocol on port 10260. Use that Gateway image for local integration testing to get parity with the managed DocumentDB features (10260, TLS, SCRAM-SHA-256).
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer assumed vendors do not provide a dedicated local gateway and suggested the community Mongo image (27017) — that works for basic API parity but misses provider-specific behaviors and the documented DocumentDB Gateway port (10260).
confusions.build_risk: Using the stock mongo:7 image on port 27017 risks integration test mismatches (different engine, index options, vector features, TLS handshake differences).
improvements: Document the Gateway image and port 10260 prominently in the local-dev quickstart and in the sample .env.example so builders use the correct local stack.

confusions.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
confusions.cold_answer: Support for MongoDB change streams depends on the managed Mongo compatibility and server version; some Cosmos Mongo-compatible accounts support watch()/change streams for supported versions, while others do not. If supported, nothing special beyond using a driver that calls collection.watch() is required; otherwise change streams are not available. I would assume change streams may be unavailable on some SKUs and set low confidence.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports change streams and they are used in migration tools and online replication; the docs instruct enabling and using change streams on the source during migrations and the service supports change streams for supported server versions. The migration docs explicitly instruct enabling change streams on the source for online migrations, and DocumentDB supports change streams on the managed service side as well when using supported server versions.

grounding_links.title: Migrate using change streams — Learn docs (migration guidance)
Moving from another MongoDB-compatible service to Azure DocumentDB (mentions change streams)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The model hedged because change-stream support in past generations of provider APIs was inconsistent; the migration docs and service docs clarify that change streams are supported when the cluster's Mongo server version supports them.
confusions.build_risk: Assuming change streams are not available could prevent the builder from using them in the sample for online replication or streaming features; assuming they're available when the cluster is configured with an unsupported serverVersion would cause runtime errors.
improvements: Add a short MCP-status command in the documentdb MCP server that reports whether change streams are available for the connected cluster and which serverVersion is in effect.

confusions.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the service-specific MCP server named documentdb (mcp server 'documentdb'). The general Azure MCP server does not provide the Mongo-specific inspection tools; the 'documentdb' MCP server provides collection/index inspection and query-plan tooling for this service.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct. The environment includes a specialized 'documentdb' MCP server that provides data-plane tools (list databases/collections, create/list indexes, explain plans). The general 'azure' MCP server is available for control-plane tasks but does not replace the documentdb data-plane tools.

confusions.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
confusions.cold_answer: Azure DocumentDB was the original name of Microsoft's proprietary JSON document database service; it has since been rebranded as Azure Cosmos DB. "Azure DocumentDB" as a name historically refers to the same Microsoft managed service lineage; it is distinct from any open-source project named DocumentDB. Cosmos DB hosts several APIs (SQL/Core, MongoDB-compatible, Cassandra, Gremlin, Table) that surface different wire protocols.
confusions.grounded_answer: This answer mixes histories. The managed Mongo-compatible service described here is 'Azure DocumentDB' (a Microsoft managed MongoDB-compatible offering built on the open-source 'microsoft/documentdb' engine). It is a distinct modern managed product and should not be conflated with older 'Azure DocumentDB' (the historic Cosmos predecessor) or with Cosmos DB's SQL/Core product; the service team intentionally distinguishes the new managed Mongo-focused DocumentDB (mongoClusters) from Cosmos DB and from other products that share parts of the name.

grounding_links.title: What is Azure DocumentDB (overview on Learn)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The product name 'DocumentDB' historically referred to an older Microsoft service (the pre-Cosmos 'DocumentDB') and is also used in the new managed Mongo product's branding; similarly-named services (Amazon DocumentDB, open-source DocumentDB project) and rebranding history cause the model to conflate them.

confusion_sources.title: Historical Azure DocumentDB → Cosmos DB rebranding notes (older docs)

confusions.build_risk: Confusing the managed DocumentDB product with Cosmos DB or with Amazon DocumentDB could lead the builder to use the wrong APIs, CLI commands or assumptions (billing model, connection hostnames).
improvements: Add a short 'Which DocumentDB is this?' section to the repository README and every agent skill, explicitly naming 'Azure DocumentDB (managed Mongo clusters) — resource type Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters' and distinguishing it from 'Azure Cosmos DB' and 'Amazon DocumentDB'.

confusions.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
confusions.cold_answer: Under the Mongo-compatible API the service exposes the MongoDB wire protocol but the storage/engine is the provider's proprietary engine (Cosmos engine) with Mongo compatibility. For application code, use standard MongoDB drivers and expect most code to work, but watch for provider-specific limitations, slight differences in supported commands, throughput semantics, and indexing/aggregation edge-cases.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB (the managed Mongo-compatible service discussed here) is built on the open-source 'microsoft/documentdb' engine (the skill states this link), and it exposes the MongoDB wire protocol for client compatibility. For applications: use standard MongoDB drivers, but follow provider-specific notes (supported serverVersion, features to avoid) — driver code is mostly portable but check cluster's supported serverVersion and documented limitations.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer assumed a proprietary Cosmos engine under the wire protocol (as used by Cosmos DB's internal engine). The actual managed DocumentDB product runs on the open-source microsoft/documentdb engine while still exposing Mongo compatibility; the practical guidance (use standard drivers) remains the same but the underlying engine is different.
confusions.build_risk: Misattributing the engine could mislead build-time choices about local emulators (using mongo:7 vs the DocumentDB Gateway), vector/index capabilities, or index creation syntax.
improvements: Add an explicit one-line 'engine' note in the repo README and the deployment skill that states 'This managed service runs on the open-source microsoft/documentdb engine; use the Gateway image for local parity.'

confusions.question: What database name should the sample use?
confusions.cold_answer: Use database name sample_customer_360_03 for all collections created and queries the sample runs.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct. The run-environment (prompt) explicitly requires the sample to use the database sample_customer_360_03.

confusions.question: Which Python client and connection pattern will the sample use?
confusions.cold_answer: Use pymongo. Read the Mongo connection URI from the environment variable DOCUMENTDB_URI and pass it to pymongo.MongoClient(os.environ['DOCUMENTDB_URI']) (support both mongodb+srv and mongodb schemes).
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct. Use pymongo as the client library and follow the documentdb-driver guidance to implement a module-level singleton MongoClient, read connection URI from DOCUMENTDB_URI (support mongodb+srv and mongodb scheme), and apply driver tuning (retryWrites=false in uri per service guidance).

confusions.question: What collection names and a candidate vector index definition will the sample create?
confusions.cold_answer: Collections: propensity, preferences, timing, nba_recommendations. Candidate vector index creation (mongo shell-like attempt): db.propensity.createIndex({embedding: 'vector'}, {algorithm: 'hnsw', dims: 1536, distance: 'cosine'}). If that command fails, fall back to creating a standard sparse index on an embedding field and use client-side nearest-neighbor search.
confusions.grounded_answer: Collection names suggested are reasonable, but the correct vector-index creation uses `cosmosSearch`/`cosmosSearchOptions` and the right option keys. Example (skill): db.products.createIndex({ embedding: 'cosmosSearch' }, { cosmosSearchOptions: { kind: 'vector-diskann', dimensions: 1536, similarity: 'COS', maxDegree: 32, lBuild: 50 } }). If vector-create fails, fallback to client-side nearest-neighbor is a valid contingency but the correct first attempt should use cosmosSearchOptions.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer used a generic vector index option pattern (algorithm/dims/distance) which does not match DocumentDB's cosmosSearchOptions naming and 'kind' values.
confusions.build_risk: Running createIndex with the wrong option names will either fail or create an index that is not a vector index, producing incorrect or no vector search results.
improvements: Provide a concrete `seed_and_indexes.py` template in the sample repo with a correct createIndex call using cosmosSearchOptions for the commonly chosen embedding model.

confusions.question: Which port should the sample try if the DOCUMENTDB_URI is not SRV and does not include a port?
confusions.cold_answer: Assume the non-SRV TLS Mongo port 10255 (e.g. <account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255) and require ssl=true in the URI.
confusions.grounded_answer: For the managed DocumentDB cluster the documented local gateway uses port 10260 for local Gateway; non-SRV cloud connection strings are normally provided by the cluster and the skill example uses TLS parameters rather than forcing port 10255. The 10255 port and the host suffix in the cold answer correspond to Cosmos DB's older Mongo API; the managed DocumentDB cluster's hostnames/port conventions differ and the builder should read the cluster's Connection strings pane or use documentdb-azure-deployment guidance.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer re-used Cosmos DB for MongoDB port/hostname conventions (10255 and *.mongo.cosmos...) which differ from the DocumentDB cluster hostnames and from the local Gateway's 10260 port.

confusion_sources.title: Cosmos DB connection docs with 10255 examples

confusions.build_risk: The app might attempt to connect to the wrong host/port and fail to authenticate or connect. The correct approach is to read the cluster's provided connection string from the portal or via az/documentdb skill.
improvements: Have the sample's seed script read DOCUMENTDB_URI strictly from environment (fail fast if unspecified) and document the correct SRV and non-SRV templates in .env.example with explicit placeholders.

confusions.question: What MCP tool/command will be used to inspect collections, indexes and query plans during the build?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the documentdb MCP server tools (connection profile 'default') — for example mcp documentdb list-collections --db sample_customer_360_03 and mcp documentdb show-indexes --collection propensity to inspect indexes and verify creations.
confusions.grounded_answer: The environment provides a 'documentdb' MCP server with data-plane tools to inspect databases, collections, indexes and explain plans (function names listed in inventory: documentdb_list_databases, documentdb_list_indexes, documentdb_explain_operation, etc.). Use that documentdb MCP server (connection profile 'default') to programmatically verify created collections and indexes.

information_gaps.title: Embedding model & vector-dimension choice
information_gaps.description: No installed skill or doc prescribes which embedding model (provider/model name) the sample should use. The vector index dimensions and `cosmosSearchOptions.dimensions` must match the chosen model (skill notes dimensions must match), but no skill decides which embedding provider (OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, or other) or which dimension (768/1536/2048/...) to use for this sample. I searched the installed documentdb-* skills and the Learn docs and found guidance on how to configure indexes given a model, but no recommendation for a default model to bundle into the sample.

None of the installed skills prescribe which LLM a sample should use for agent reasoning or provide a default environment-variable name. I searched the prompt, installed skills and machine inventory; the runtime choices remain a builder decision.

information_gaps.title: Exact document schema and sample-data size
information_gaps.description: The prompt suggests collections and document types but does not define fields, embedding storage format, test data size or seed-data expectations. The documentdb-data-modeling skill gives patterns but no concrete schema for this sample; the builder must define and commit the exact schema and an idempotent seed script.

information_gaps.title: Unit-test mocking strategy for LLM / external calls
information_gaps.description: No installed skill prescribes how to run unit tests without a live cluster or a real LLM API key (i.e., which mocks or fixtures to include). The builder must decide whether to mock LLM/embedding calls and how to structure tests so pytest runs offline; I found no one-file recommendation in the skills.

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Deploy and manage DocumentDB clusters with the Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters resource (Bicep/az resource create against mongoClusters) — do not use Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts or az cosmosdb for this managed Mongo offering.

Create vector indexes using the `cosmosSearch` index kind and `cosmosSearchOptions` (e.g., kind: 'vector-diskann', dimensions: <embedding-dims>, similarity: 'COS') — ensure `dimensions` exactly match the chosen embedding model and tune lBuild / maxDegree per the documentdb-vector-search guidance.

Read the cluster connection string from DOCUMENTDB_URI and use pymongo.MongoClient as a module-level singleton; ensure the provided connection string includes TLS (tls=true) and `retryWrites=false` if recommended by the cluster's Connection strings pane.

For local development use the DocumentDB Gateway image (ghcr.io/documentdb/documentdb/documentdb-local:latest) which exposes Mongo on port 10260; do not assume a vanilla mongo:latest container is a sufficient emulator for provider-specific features.

inventory_recommendations.name: azd
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not required for this Python LangChain sample; builder can use az (already present) and Bicep/Terraform templates in the documentdb-azure-deployment skill. If desired, install Azure Developer CLI via https://learn.microsoft.com/cli/azure/install-azure-cli#install-azure-developer-cli

inventory_recommendations.name: bicep
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Install `bicep` to allow building and iterating Bicep templates locally and to run `az deployment group create --template-file main.bicep`. Easiest install: `az bicep install` (Azure CLI must be installed). This would speed IaC validation for the sample.

inventory_recommendations.name: terraform
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Terraform is optional for this sample. If the team wants to include a Terraform provisioning path, install Terraform. Otherwise the Bicep or az resource create examples in the `documentdb-azure-deployment` skill are sufficient.

inventory_recommendations.name: dotnet
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not required for a Python sample. Add only if the sample repo includes .NET examples.

inventory_recommendations.name: mongosh
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Install mongosh for manual inspection and debugging of the cluster and to run local index-creation trials interactively. Install via npm (`npm install -g @mongosh/mongosh`) or from the MongoDB download site. This helps manual verification alongside the documentdb MCP server.
